## Reminder of the Missing Data Problem

::: smaller-text
-   **Not random variables:**

    -   $y_i$ = survey outcome of interest for unit $i$, only observed
        for respondents

    -   $\mathbf{x}_i$ = vector of information known about unit $i$,
        observed for ALL sampled units\
        *(design information, information on the sampling frame, or
        information about the interview process)*

-   **Random variables:**

    -   $Z_i$ = selection indicator for unit $i$

        -   $\pi_i = P(Z_i=1)$ = selection probability
            [(known!)]{.alert}

    -   $R_i$ = response indicator for unit $i$

        -   $\phi_i = P(R_i=1)$ = probability unit $i$ responds =
            response propensity [(unknown)]{.alert2}

-   Three types of missing data mechanisms:

-   **MCAR**: $P(R_i=1 | y_i, \mathbf{x}_i) = P(R_i=1)$ ← missingness
    doesn't depend on $y$ or $x$

-   **MAR**: $P(R_i=1 | y_i, \mathbf{x}_i) = P(R_i=1|\mathbf{x}_i)$ ←
    missingness doesn't depend on $y$

-   **MNAR**: $P(R_i=1 | y_i, \mathbf{x}_i)$ ← missingness depends on
    $y$, possibly also $x$

-   Usually MCAR does not hold (often we have visible differences
    between respondents and nonrespondents), and we assume MAR

-   MNAR not testable given observed data
:::

## Adjusting Sample Weights for Unit Nonresponse

-   If $R_i \perp \!\!\! \perp Z_i$ (response is independent of
    selection into the sample), then: $$\begin{aligned}
    P(\text{unit }i & \text{ selected in sample and responds}) \\
    & = P(\text{unit }i\text{ selected in sample})\times P(\text{unit }i\text{ responds}|\text{unit }i\text{ selected in sample}) \\
    & = P(\text{unit }i\text{ selected in sample})\times P(\text{unit }i\text{ responds}) \\
    & = \pi_i \phi_i
    \end{aligned}$$

-   We adjust the weights by [estimating the $\phi_i$]{.alert} and then
    assigning the weights:
    $$w_i = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\pi_i \hat{\phi}_i} & \text{for respondents }(R_i=1) \\ 0 & \text{for nonrespondents }(R_i=0)
    \end{cases}$$

-   $\hat{\phi}_i$ must be estimated -- and info for doing so may be
    limited for some surveys

-   Weighting methods assume that response probabilities can be
    estimated [from variables known for all units]{.alert2}

    -   $P(R_i=1 | y_i, \mathbf{x}_i) = P(R_i=1|\mathbf{x}_i)$
    -   Thus they assume [MAR]{.alert2} data

## Weighting Class Adjustments

::: smaller-text
-   Simplest weighting adjustment method (but very, very commonly used)

1.  Create **weighting adjustment classes** = groups of respondents and
    nonrespondents based on variables observed for both

2.  Estimate response probability within each class with either the
    unweighted or weighted response rate:

$$\hat{\phi}_c = \frac{\text{number of respondents in class } c}{\text{number of selected units in class }c} \quad \text{ or } \quad \hat{\phi}_c = \frac{\text{sum of weights for respondents in class } c}{\text{sum of weights for selected sample in class }c}$$

3.  Use these estimated response propensities for each class,
    $\hat{\phi}_c$, to adjust the weights for the respondents as:
    $$\tilde{w}_i = w_i \frac{1}{\hat{\phi}_i} = \frac{1}{\pi_i \hat{\phi}_i}$$

-   Notes:

    -   Implicitly assumes probability of response is the **same for all
        units within each class**

    -   All weights are **up-weighted** since response propensities are
        between 0 and 1

    -   This is **different than poststratification** (with complete
        response) where some units get up-weighted and some
        down-weighted
:::

## Example: Weight Adjustments {.pause}

:::::: {columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   Population of $N=1{,}000$ graduates with PhDs in
    statistics/biostatistics in past year

-   SRS of $n=10$ with response rate of 6/10 = 60%

-   Type of degree (stat vs. biostat) is on the sampling frame

-   Type of job is on the survey

-   Without adjustment, estimated proportion of graduates in Academic
    jobs is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
:::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: smaller-text
| ID  | Biostat | Academic | Base Weight $(w_i)$ |
|:---:|:-------:|:--------:|:-------------------:|
|  1  |    0    |    1     |         100         |
|  2  |    1    |          |         100         |
|  3  |    0    |          |         100         |
|  4  |    1    |    1     |         100         |
|  5  |    0    |    0     |         100         |
|  6  |    1    |    0     |         100         |
|  7  |    0    |    0     |         100         |
|  8  |    0    |          |         100         |
|  9  |    1    |    1     |         100         |
| 10  |    0    |          |         100         |
:::
::::
::::::

. . .

-   Don't like this estimate? We have two choices:

    1.  Treat the entire sample as one adjustment class, and upweight
        all 6 respondents the same (MCAR)

    2.  Group the sample by degree type, and apply a different
        adjustment factor to biostat and stat (MAR)

        -   Specifically, assume missingness depends on degree type

## Example: Option 1

::: {.smaller-text}
-   **Option 1:** Assume MCAR and use one big weighting adjustment class

-   Estimated probability of response = $\hat{\phi}_i$ = same for all
    units
:::

::: even-smaller-text
|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|
|  |  |  | **Base Weight** | **Response Propensity** | **Adjusted Weight** |
| ID | Biostat | Academic | $w_i$ | $\hat{\phi}_i$ | $\tilde{w}_i = w_i / \hat{\phi}_i$ |
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 100 | 6/10 = 0.6 | 100/0.6 = 166.67 |
| 2 | 1 |  | 100 |  | 0 |
| 3 | 0 |  | 100 |  | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 100 | 0.6 | 166.67 |
| 5 | 0 | 0 | 100 | 0.6 | 166.67 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 100 | 0.6 | 166.67 |
| 7 | 0 | 0 | 100 | 0.6 | 166.67 |
| 8 | 0 |  | 100 |  | 0 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 100 | 0.6 | 166.67 |
| 10 | 0 |  | 100 |  | 0 |
|  |  | **Sum:** | 1000 | **Sum:** | 1000 |
: {tbl-colwidths="[10,10,10,23,23,24]"}
:::

::: even-smaller-text
|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|
|  |  |  | **Base Weight** | **Response Propensity** | **Adjusted Weight** |
| ID | Biostat | Academic | $w_i$ | $\hat{\phi}_i$ | $\tilde{w}_i = w_i / \hat{\phi}_i$ |
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 100 | 6/10 = 0.6 | 100/0.6 = 166.67 |
| 2 | 1 |  | 100 |  | 0 |
| 3 | 0 |  | 100 |  | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 100 | 0.6 | 166.67 |
| 5 | 0 | 0 | 100 | 0.6 | 166.67 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 100 | 0.6 | 166.67 |
| 7 | 0 | 0 | 100 | 0.6 | 166.67 |
| 8 | 0 |  | 100 |  | 0 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 100 | 0.6 | 166.67 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[10,10,10,23,23,24]"}

<br>

::: {.smaller-text}

-   Estimated total number of grads in Academic jobs: $\hat{t} = \sum_{i \in \S} \tilde{w}_i y_i = 166.67(1) + 166.67(1) + 166.67(0) + \cdots = 500$
-   Estimated proportion of grads in Academic jobs: $\hat{p} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \S} \tilde{w}_i y_i}{\sum_{i \in \S} \tilde{w}_i} = \frac{500}{1000} = 0.5$
-   Estimate is the same as without adjustment ("complete case") --
    assumed MCAR!

:::

## Example (con't)

-   Do you like this adjustment?

-   Look at the breakdown of who responded:

| Type of Degree | Number in Sample | Number Responded | Response Rate |
|:---------------|:----------------:|:----------------:|:-------------:|
| Biostatistics  |        4         |        3         |   3/4 = 75%   |
| Statistics     |        6         |        3         |   3/6 = 50%   |

-   Response rate is **different** for biostat and stat graduates
    (different by degree type)!

**Not MCAR!**

-   Would our estimate based on this weight adjustment (assuming MCAR)
    be too high? Too small? Just right?

<br>

-   What if there was no relationship between degree type and having an
    academic job?

<br>

-   A better approach is to form weighting adjustment classes based on
    degree type

## Example (con't)

-   **Option 2:** Assume and create weighting adjustment classes based
    on degree

-   Estimated probability of response = $\hat{\phi}_i$ separately
    estimated for biostat, stat

::: center
|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|------------|------------|------------|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|
|  |  |  | Base Weight | Response Propensity | Adjusted Weight |
| ID | Biostat | Academic | $w_i$ | $\hat{\phi}_i$ | $\tilde{w}_i = w_i / \hat{\phi}_i$ |
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 100 | 3/6 = 0.5 | 100/0.5 = 200 |
| 3 | 0 |  | 100 |  | 0 |
| 5 | 0 | 0 | 100 | 0.5 | 200 |
| 7 | 0 | 0 | 100 | 0.5 | 200 |
| 8 | 0 |  | 100 |  | 0 |
| 10 | 0 |  | 100 |  | 0 |
| 2 | 1 |  | 100 |  | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 100 | 3/4 = 0.75 | 100/0.75 = 133.33 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 100 | 0.75 | 133.33 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 100 | 0.75 | 133.33 |
|  |  |  | Sum: 1000 |  | Sum: 1000 |
:::

-   Estimated total number of graduates who are in Academic jobs:
    $$\hat{t} = \sum_{i \in \S} \tilde{w}_i y_i = 200(1) + 200(0) + \cdots + 133.33(1) = 466.67$$

-   Estimated proportion of graduates who are in Academic jobs:
    $$\hat{p} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \S} \tilde{w}_i y_i}{\sum_{i \in \S} \tilde{w}_i} = \frac{466.67}{1000} = 0.47$$

-   Estimates are different than under MCAR!

## Choosing Variables for Adjustments

-   Limited info might make the choice simple

-   Can only use variables that are observed for both respondents and
    nonrespondents

-   Limited to information on the sampling frame and design variables

    -   Ex: Ohio Medicaid Assessment Survey (OMAS)

        -   RDD phone survey, only info about nonrespondents is the
            stratum they are from

        -   Thus adjustment classes are the strata (only choice!)

-   In multi-stage surveys, nonresponse can happen at different stages,
    thus can make different adjustment classes for each level

    -   Ex: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES)

        -   First dwelling units are screened (to enumerate people in
            them), then sampled people are interviewed, then interviewed
            people are given a medical exam

        -   Nonresponse can happen at any stage -- refuse to participate
            in the screening, or the interview, or the medical exam

        -   Adjustment classes for nonresponse at screener are limited
            to design info\
            (i.e., use census tract/segment as adjustment class)

        -   Adjustment classes for interview can include screener info

        -   Adjustment classes for medical exam can include interview
            info

## Choosing Variables for Adjustments (con't)

-   **Overall goal: choose variables that are associated with** $R_i$
    and with $y_i$

-   In other words, weighting classes should be formed so that:

    -   Units within each class are as similar as possible with respect
        to $y_i$, and

    -   Response propensities similar within class but (may) vary from
        class to class

-   Impact on bias and variance when constructing classes using
    variables that have: [^1]

[^1]: Table 1 in: Little RJA & Vartivarian S (2005), Does Weighting for
    Nonresponse Increase the Variance of Survey Means? *Survey
    Methodology*, 31, 161-168.

::: center
|                        |      |                        |                        |
|------------------|------------------|:----------------:|------------------|
|                        |      | Association with $y_i$ |                        |
|                        |      |          Low           | High                   |
| Association with $R_i$ | Low  |        Bias: --        | Bias: --               |
|                        |      |      Variance: --      | Variance: $\downarrow$ |
|                        | High |        Bias: --        | Bias: $\downarrow$     |
|                        |      |  Variance: $\uparrow$  | Variance: $\downarrow$ |
:::

-   Key points:

    -   Only get bias reduction if classes are constructed with
        variables related to $y_i$

    -   "Punishment" for using variables not associated with $y_i$ can
        be an increase in variance

-   Obvious problem: All surveys have more than one $y$ that they care
    about!

-   But -- only one set of adjusted weights!

## Activity 18.1

Nonresponse Weight Adjustments

## More Practical Details on Weighting Adjustments

-   Resulting data are analyzed as if the adjusted weights were the base
    weights\
    (i.e., no special analysis method needed)

-   If \>50% nonresponse in a class, weights would be multiplied by a
    factor greater than 2 -- and this is generally avoided

    -   Option 1: Collapse classes together until have enough
        respondents

    -   Option 2: Weight trimming, by choosing a max value for the
        weights and truncating any adjusted weights above this value

-   Categorical variables can be easily used to form classes, but
    continuous variables need to be categorized (no strict rule about
    how)

-   More complex weighting adjustments are possible -- fancier methods
    to estimate $\hat{\phi}_i$

    -   Ex: Logistic regression with $R_i$ as the outcome

        -   Predictors are variables available for both respondents and
            nonrespondents (those available for creating classes)

        -   Each respondent has a predicted propensity from the model,
            $\hat{\phi}_i$

        -   Adjusted weight is (as usual)
            $\tilde{w}_i = w_i/\hat{\phi}_i$

        -   Or -- create classes based on grouping units with similar
            $\hat{\phi}_i$

## Combining Nonresponse Adjustments with Other Weight Adjustments

-   When adjusting the weights for nonresponse, you can think of it as
    multiplying each weight by an adjustment factor, where
    $$\tilde{w}_i = w_i \times \frac{1}{\hat{\phi}_i} = w_i \times \text{(adjustment factor)}$$

-   This may remind you of poststratification:
    $$w_{hj}^{PS} = w_{hj} \times \frac{\text{Population total in post-stratum}~h}{\text{Estimated total in post-stratum}~h}  = w_{hj} \times \frac{N_h}{\widehat{N}_h}$$

-   Weighting adjustments for nonresponse can be combined with
    poststratification:

    1.  First, make nonresponse adjustments to the weights

    2.  Second, use poststratification or raking to ensure that weights
        sum to population totals for key quantities (for which you know
        the population totals)

-   The adjustment factors just all get multiplied together:
    $$\tilde{w}_i = w_i \times \frac{1}{\hat{\phi}_i} \times \frac{N_h}{\widehat{N}_h}$$
    where unit $i$ belongs to poststratum $h$

## Combining (con't)

-   Key difference between nonresponse weight adjustments and
    poststratification/raking:

    -   For **nonresponse weight adjustments**, you must have the
        variables that create the adjustment cells **observed for all
        sampled units, respondents and nonrespondents**

    -   For **poststratification/raking**, you need the **population
        totals for variables that are observed for respondents**
        (individual nonrespondent data not needed)

-   Most often, both are done -- nonresponse first, then
    poststratification/raking (also commonly called calibration)

<br>

-   Think of it this way:

    -   **Nonresponse weight adjustments** are made to align the
        respondent sample with the originally selected sample (i.e.,
        make the respondent sample look like the full sample)

    -   **Poststratification/Raking/Calibration** are then made to align
        the resulting sample with the target population

## Combining (con't)

-   Other weight adjustments are commonly done in certain scenarios as
    well, e.g.,:

    -   **Ineligibility adjustment** -- some sampled units may not be
        eligible (e.g., phone number that does not belong to a person in
        the target population), so adjust weights to reallocate the
        weights for these ineligible units

    -   **Dual-frame adjustment** -- for surveys that use two frames
        (e.g., cell phone frame and landline frame), adjust for the fact
        that some units could appear on both frames and thus have a
        higher chance of selection into the sample

    -   **Number of phone numbers adjustment** -- in phone surveys,
        people with more than one phone number have higher probability
        of selection (but don't know who has multiple numbers at the
        design stage), so adjust weights accordingly (higher probability
        of selection $\rightarrow$ lower weight)
